sources.title: Are Mutants a Valid Substitute for Real Faults in Software Testing?

reviewed_source.edition: Author PDF, FSE'14 (Hong Kong, 16–22 November 2014), ISBN 978-1-4503-3056-5
reviewed_source.attribution_note: Six authors on the PDF title page; no DOI printed.
reviewed_source.license: No explicit redistribution license established; public metadata and summaries do not redistribute the source.

sources.application: Grounds treating mechanical mutants as a secondary, imperfect proxy and model-written faults as primary.

source_locators.supports: 73% of the studied real faults are coupled to mutants from commonly used operators; 27% are not, and about 17% are coupled to no mutant.
source_locators.boundary: Java programs from Defects4J with developer-written tests; coupling rates need not hold for Python functions or model-written faults.

source_locators.supports: Mutant detection is positively correlated with real-fault detection across test suites, with coverage controlled.
source_locators.boundary: A correlation across suites, not a guarantee that a suite killing mutants catches a given real fault.

artifact_links.expected_text:
\textbf{Why model-written faults.} Hand-made faults risk measuring what the study
author expected. Mechanical mutants are standard but are an imperfect proxy for
real faults~\cite[\S3]{mutants}. We instead use mistakes that code models actually
made: EvalPlus showed that many solutions accepted by HumanEval's original tests
are wrong~\cite[\S1; \S3]{evalplus}. Each such solution is a fault that a
competent-looking test suite missed.

As a secondary population we apply single-site mutation operators (relational,
arithmetic, logical, constant and condition changes) to each reference and keep
mutants with the same property. Mutant detection correlates with real-fault
detection in Java projects, but about a quarter of real faults are not coupled to
common mutants~\cite[\S3]{mutants}; we therefore treat model-written faults as
primary.

\hypertarget{related}{}
\textbf{6. Related work.}
\textbf{Test adequacy and faults.} EvalPlus extends HumanEval with inputs from
model-written seeds and type-aware mutation, and shows that pass rates fall when
the extra inputs are used~\cite[\S2.1; \S3]{evalplus}; we reuse its inputs as the
ground truth that defines a fault. Just et al.\ find mutant detection positively
correlated with real-fault detection, while about a quarter of real faults are not
coupled to common mutants~\cite[\S3.1--3.3]{mutants}. CodeT uses model-generated
tests to rank model-generated programs~\cite[\S2.1--2.2]{codet}; here tests are the
product and are scored against faults the tester never sees.

sources.title: Predictive Representations of State
sources.author_label: M. L. Littman, R. S. Sutton and S. Singh

reviewed_source.edition: NIPS 2001 proceedings, volume 14, pp. 1555–1561; supplied 14-physical-page PDF
reviewed_source.attribution_note: All three authors are verified on the PDF title page; the proceedings HTML/BibTeX omits Singh. Physical PDF pages 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 are content pages 1–7 and proceedings pp. 1555–1561; every even physical page is blank.
reviewed_source.license: No explicit redistribution license established; public metadata and summaries do not redistribute the supplied PDF.

sources.application: Conceptual context: future-test probabilities motivate predictive state. Zenith’s implemented deterministic rational-linear learner is not the stochastic PSR construction or evidence of its proposed learning advantages.

source_locators.locator: §1, Eqs. (1)–(3); physical PDF pp. 5, 7 / content pp. 3–4 / proceedings pp. 1557–1558
source_locators.supports: A predictive state determines probabilities of all future action-observation tests; conditioning uses a normalized ratio of linear functions.
source_locators.boundary: A linear PSR does not have an unnormalized linear state update. Its stochastic sufficiency requirement does not certify Zenith’s finite deterministic checks.

source_locators.locator: §2, Theorem 1 and Lemma 1; physical PDF pp. 7, 9, 11 / content pp. 4–6 / proceedings pp. 1558–1560
source_locators.supports: A finite POMDP has a linear PSR using no more tests than states in its minimal POMDP; the construction uses the supplied POMDP model.
source_locators.boundary: This is a known-model representation result, not a black-box acquisition algorithm or a theorem that arbitrary software has finite rank.

source_locators.locator: §3; physical PDF pp. 11, 13 / content pp. 6–7 / proceedings pp. 1560–1561
source_locators.supports: Learnability and generalization are proposed advantages for future investigation.
source_locators.boundary: The paper does not establish empirical learning, cross-task question transfer or recursive self-improvement.

artifact_links.expected_text:
\hypertarget{evolve}{}
\textbf{Continuation learning.}
Predictive state representations encode stochastic state through probabilities
of future tests. The cited theorem constructs a representation from a known
finite POMDP; it does not supply a black-box learning algorithm~\cite[Theorem 1; \S2]{psr}.
Our continuation learner instead fits exact integer observations in a
rational-linear model. The conceptual connection is the use of future tests
to distinguish histories.

sources.title: Exactly Learning Weighted Automata over a Field

reviewed_source.edition: Supplied three-page Oxford teaching note; no printed date or byline
reviewed_source.attribution_note: Attribution to James Worrell comes from his Oxford teaching index, https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/people/james.worrell/lectures.html. PDF build metadata dated 23 February 2017 is not a verified publication year. The note credits the algorithm to Beimel, Bergadano, Bshouty, Kushilevitz and Varricchio (JACM 2000).
reviewed_source.license: No explicit redistribution license established; only metadata and source-located summaries are published.

sources.application: Implemented antecedent: Zenith’s continuation learner fits a weighted-linear observation table and retains paired history/test rank witnesses. Its finite challenge sequence replaces the note’s global equivalence oracle, so the repair restores an established invariant without proving general source equivalence.

source_locators.locator: pp. 1–2, field-valued series and unnumbered observation-table construction
source_locators.supports: Histories index Hankel rows, continuations index columns, and a square full-rank table determines transition maps through H M(σ) = Hσ.
source_locators.boundary: The model class and exact field arithmetic are assumptions; dimension bounds are relative to this linear representation.

source_locators.supports: Counterexample refinement adds both an access history and a distinguishing continuation, increasing the observation table’s rank.
source_locators.boundary: Keeping a question alone does not preserve its rank witness. Zenith’s regression checks this established requirement; it is not a new learning theorem.

source_locators.locator: p. 1, membership and equivalence queries; Proposition 1, pp. 2–3
source_locators.supports: Exact membership answers and a counterexample whenever the hypothesis is globally wrong support the learning procedure.
source_locators.boundary: Finite challenges cannot supply that equivalence guarantee; the note does not establish transfer savings or lifetime economy for native software.

artifact_links.expected_text:
Access histories $h$ and continuation tests $t$ index an observation table,
$H_{h,t}=f(ht)$, for deterministic observations $f$. Given exact field-valued
answers and a square full-rank table, a counterexample supplies a history--test
pair whose nonzero residual increases the rank~\cite[Proposition 1, pp.\ 2--3]{weighted}.
Our repair preserves the paired access history and distinguishing test required
by this construction. Across eight native configurations both the repaired
refinement and a generic bank of one-symbol questions complete every fit;
generic questions cost 11,379 acquisition source executions versus 11,395, and
later finite checks retain errors. Useful questions have not yet made that
architecture economical.

sources.title: Effective Test Generation Using Pre-trained Large Language Models and Mutation Testing

reviewed_source.edition: arXiv source bundle as served by arxiv.org e-print on 19 October 2026; version number not printed in the bundle; Elsevier cas-dc class
reviewed_source.attribution_note: Authors read from the LaTeX source; journal venue not printed and not asserted.
reviewed_source.license: No explicit redistribution license established; public metadata and summaries do not redistribute the source.

sources.application: Within-program precedent: surviving mutants of the same program are fed back into the test-generation prompt.

source_locators.supports: MuTAP augments the initial prompt with the initial tests and a surviving mutant of the same program under test.
source_locators.boundary: The prompt includes the program's source; experience is not carried to other programs, and the mutants that guide the prompt are also those scored.

artifact_links.expected_text:
\textbf{Mutation-guided generation.} MuTAP returns surviving mutants of the same
program to the prompt so that the next round of tests kills them~\cite[\S3.4]{mutap}.
Meta's ACH asks a model to write faults of a stated concern and then tests that
catch them, and deploys the tests~\cite[\S1; \S2]{ach}. ACH is the closest precedent
for our imagined-fault condition; both MuTAP and ACH work within one program,
whereas we ask whether experience transfers to unseen programs.

sources.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning

reviewed_source.edition: arXiv source bundle as served by arxiv.org e-print on 19 October 2026; version number not printed in the bundle; neurips_2023 style with the preprint option
reviewed_source.attribution_note: Figures quoted only where they match this revision.
reviewed_source.license: No explicit redistribution license established; public metadata and summaries do not redistribute the source.

sources.application: Within-task precedent: written reflections reused on later trials of the same task.

source_locators.supports: Reflexion converts binary or scalar feedback into a textual summary that is added to the next episode's context.
source_locators.boundary: No transfer of reflections to unseen tasks is reported.

source_locators.supports: Memory holds a few reflections (one for programming), and learning is measured over repeated trials of the same task; the programming evaluator is the agent's own tests.
source_locators.boundary: Repeated trials on one task differ from transfer to new programs.

artifact_links.expected_text:
\textbf{Learning from experience without changing weights.} Reflexion turns
feedback into written reflections reused on later trials of the same
task~\cite[\S1; \S4.3]{reflexion}. ExpeL gathers insights and successful
trajectories on training tasks and evaluates on tasks not used for gathering; it
finds distilled insights and retrieved examples complementary, with their
relative value depending on the task~\cite[\S5.1--5.2]{expel}. Dynamic Cheatsheet
keeps a curated memory at test time; appending the whole raw history did worse
than curation, and generic structured instructions alone already helped~\cite[\S2.3; \S4.3]{cheatsheet}.
ACE evolves such contexts as itemised playbooks and reports that rewriting a
whole context can collapse it~\cite[\S2.2; \S4.3]{ace}. None of these evaluates
software testing. Our record and playbook conditions apply the idea to the choice
of test inputs, and the generic-advice condition separates experience from
instruction.

sources.title: Learning to Fuzz from Symbolic Execution with Application to Smart Contracts

reviewed_source.attribution_note: Author list and title verified on the supplied first page. One-based PDF p. 1 corresponds to proceedings p. 531. Publication metadata cross-checked against the authors’ SRI Lab publication page.
reviewed_source.license: Author PDF carries ACM personal/classroom copying and attribution conditions; no blanket paper redistribution is asserted. The separate ILF code repository uses Apache-2.0.

sources.application: Context and evaluation precedent: expensive symbolic demonstrations train a reusable fuzzing policy. Zenith does not implement ILF’s neural policy training or Ethereum representation; any future testing comparison must include acquisition and training as well as deployment.

source_locators.locator: PDF p. 7, §4.2 “Learning from Expert”; pp. 7–9, §§5.1–5.2, Table 2 and Algorithm 1
source_locators.supports: A symbolic expert supplies coverage-improving transaction sequences; imitation learning updates neural policy weights, and the deployed policy consumes contract/history features.
source_locators.boundary: Runtime history adaptation is distinct from retraining. Ethereum-specific features are authored; the paper does not discover arbitrary representation boundaries or improve its own training algorithm.

source_locators.supports: The evaluation deduplicates the collected contracts and uses random five-fold contract-level cross-validation on 18,496 contracts.
source_locators.boundary: Exact deduplication and contract withholding do not establish a project/lineage, functionality-family, chronological or unrelated-domain split.

source_locators.supports: The source separates symbolic expert execution, policy training and fast deployment; the useful result is amortization on further contracts.
source_locators.boundary: Deployment throughput is not total lifetime cost. Coverage and detector results are empirical, domain-specific and do not establish correctness or vulnerability completeness.

sources.author_label: J. Altmayer Pizzorno and E. D. Berger

source_locators.supports: Source and coverage context guide test generation; execution errors and missing coverage prompt bounded follow-up dialogue, retaining passing tests that add coverage.

sources.application: Proposed protocol: freeze acquired meta-agents and compare their improvements on identical fresh solvers, selecting children before untouched evaluation. Current Zenith has no learned self-improver; the source’s architecture and meta-evaluation are precedents, not local results.

source_locators.supports: Task and meta-agent code share an editable program and archive; main experiments keep task distribution, parent selection and evaluation protocols fixed.
source_locators.boundary: Self-editing code is not unrestricted self-modification. Fixed foundation models do not include downstream robotics policies trained by RL.

source_locators.locator: paper.tex:254–283, §5.2; paper.tex:707–753, appendices app:genk-metric and app:transfer-selection
source_locators.supports: Improvement@k holds the meta-agent fixed, and validation-selected task agents test the usefulness of source-acquired improvement machinery in a new domain.
source_locators.boundary: The transfer carries both task and meta implementations, and initial format failures create headroom. Follow the main development/validation-before-test protocol rather than selecting the maximum test score from the appendix display.

source_locators.supports: Continued runs compare transferred and initial agents; the 200-iteration transfer-versus-fresh result is explicitly not statistically significant.
source_locators.boundary: The reported 0.640 versus 0.610 comparison has p > 0.05; stronger task-agent improvements and qualitative memory examples do not by themselves establish accelerating recursive self-improvement.
